title: 2007 Study Abroad Report: "Returning to Being a Baby"
paragraphs: Period: March 26 to June 15, 2007. Location: University of Pennsylvania, Pennsylvania, United States. Clerkship sites: Division of Pulmonary Medicine, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia; Division of Cardiology, The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia; CHOP Newborn Care at Pennsylvania Hospital, Pennsylvania Hospital

That day I left Nagoya with my chest full of expectation and anxiety, my suitcase full of excess luggage, and a show of bravado as best I could manage. On the plane, some words suddenly came to my mind. "Until now you have been protected by those around you, and everything that was 'normal' without your even being aware of it will no longer be so. Think of it as a chance to create 'yourself' again, and do your best." These were the words the Dean gave me before I left. At the time I did not yet understand how deep they were.

CHOP. The Children's Hospital of Philadelphia (hereafter CHOP), where I had the opportunity to do my clerkship, is both an independent children's hospital and the pediatrics department of the University of Pennsylvania. With a history of 150 years, it is the core of a health care network that extends not only across Pennsylvania but also to the neighboring states of New Jersey and Delaware. It is one of the leading research institutions in the United States, has every imaginable clinical department, and is a hospital very well endowed in both facilities and staff. It is also an excellent educational institution, where many residents (junior trainees), fellows (senior trainees) and medical students are taught every day. I spent the first two months in the pulmonology and cardiology departments at CHOP, and the third month in Newborn Care at Pennsylvania Hospital.

Bewilderment. At the children's hospital there were children and families with more varied problems than I had imagined. There was no child hospitalized for a cold. In pulmonology, most of the inpatients had cystic fibrosis (CF), but in consults I also often saw so-called technology-dependent children, such as those with mental retardation/cerebral palsy (MR/CP) or neuromuscular disease who had a tracheotomy. Connected to many monitors, with many openings in their bodies, with tubes inserted. Unable to support their own weight by themselves. Unable to move freely. Always needing someone at their side. Unable to convey what they wanted to say. Day after day I met children with complex problems, and honestly I was very shocked. What is advanced medicine? Who is advanced medicine for? Around the same time, a report meeting on training in developing countries by CHOP residents was held. A contaminated living environment, limited access to hospitals, shortages of medical supplies, a lack of education for the people, a lack of knowledge and awareness among the people. Just from the medical side, the problems were piled up high. It is not rare for children to lose their lives to diseases that, by our standards, should be curable. Aren't there children who need medical resources even more? This conflict grew bigger inside me day by day, and gradually I came to spend less time in patients' rooms. Because of my own doubts about advanced medicine, I had begun to avoid facing the patients.

A smile I encountered. At that time I sent an email to a friend. "I'm worn out by these somewhat overwhelming days." The day after I sent that email, I happened to meet in the corridor a patient I knew from the consult and his family. "Hi!" said the patient. "Hey," I said. "If you stay in the room all the time you feel suffocated, so we're out for a walk, a walk," his mother, who was attending him, said to me. He was a man in his early thirties with Duchenne muscular dystrophy. It seemed that at baseline it was almost impossible for him to move by himself, and he could barely control his facial muscles. He was hospitalized with a pain of unclear focus as his chief complaint, but it was hard to control and was not improving. He was so exhausted that he could hardly keep his eyes open. We started by talking about his condition, then, "Naomi, you're from Japan, right?", about Japan, then, "Actually I had a Japanese friend too," about his friend. He spun his words carefully, very carefully. His mother filled in the places that needed explanation. Then, as I had to go to the next patient, I said, "Better get going. See you again soon, 'k?" and he gave me a smile and said, "See ya." The patient's smile at that moment was very gentle, and I instinctively felt that it was the most "beautiful" thing. That night, my friend's reply said this. "I don't think advanced medicine is all bad. But I do wish some of that passion would be shared a little with the children in developing countries." And it continued, "There are also patients you could not have met without advanced medical technology, and smiles you could not have seen." In those short words I felt my friend's warmth. At the same time, the face of the patient I had met during the day came to mind. And I realized. It had all been my own selfish assumption. There is not just one set of values. Trying to measure everything by my own yardstick was nothing but arrogance. It was disrespectful to the patients who were living with all their might and to the love of the families who were trying with all their might to protect them. The meaning of "living" must surely be different for each person. I do not know how much help I can be, but I will make an effort to face each patient and think together with them about this question that has no answer. Disparities in medical care also arise from economic reasons, political reasons and the circumstances of each country. If you look at medicine in developing countries through the eyes of that region, it is surely progressing. Perhaps what matters is to look a little ahead while providing the best care possible now. In this way, I, who had been stopped by the "significance of advanced medicine," was able to take a step forward thanks to my friend's simple words and, above all, the smile of the patient who spoke to me in the corridor. It was a small event, but it felt as if my body suddenly became lighter.

Meeting the ICN. The last rotation I was allowed to do was the Intensive Care Nursery (hereafter ICN) at Pennsylvania Hospital. It was almost my first time in a newborn unit, and on the first day I even felt as if I had wandered into another dimension. The air inside the unit was quiet. All I could hear was the alarms of the monitors. The residents there hardly moved, tiny, tiny lives that seemed they could fit in the palm of a hand. Some babies had faces that looked as if they came out of an embryology textbook. I was timid even when taking physical findings. In the departments up to then there had been clear "admission goals," whereas the care in the ICN seemed at first glance to have no goal. It is not the case that the patient is discharged once their condition is raised to a certain line. For the first week I simply listened to the nurses' presentations. One day, casually, I peeked into the isolette of a baby on the next team. It was a week since I had last seen her. And I noticed. ...She's growing!!! That is of course natural. It would be a problem if she did not grow, and conversely there are problems that arise precisely because she grows. Depending on the condition, "growth" can feel like a "time limit." Even so, she had indeed become bigger. Skin that used to get sore at the slightest touch now had a faint covering of downy hair, and her body had grown a size larger. At that moment my whole body trembled. She no longer seemed like an "ICN patient" but like one precious individual. I felt as if I had touched the tenacity of life. "What you can do is learn from the patients. That is all." I savored these words said to me by a teacher at my home university whom I respect. With a body of only 700 g, she taught me something important. That "I am alive."

Living with a feeling of "thank you." As for the sense of unease I had at the beginning of the clerkship, that "I can't see the goal," a nurse practitioner explained to me, "The goal is the same for everyone. It is to stand on the starting line. Until they get there, there are babies who go down various roads and run into various problems, but our role is to help them get over them." Thanks also to the kindness of the Course Director, who said, "Ask whatever you want to know. Tell me whatever you want to try," I went to see my assigned babies first thing every morning so as to live up to it. I asked the night-shift nurses how they were, took physical findings and checked the test data. I confirmed the treatment being given according to the protocol and the tests scheduled for that day. If there was a problem, I raised it at rounds and made a plan together. It was a clerkship faithful to the basics. A very luxurious clerkship. I was given the opportunity to ask questions whenever I wondered about something, and when there was time I could also receive short lectures on topics I was interested in. From around this time, I also began to look at my daily life afresh. "I am a being who can do nothing alone, and I can live only because others are there. Nothing is 'a matter of course'; it is the result of someone using their own time for it." Toward everything, feelings of "I am grateful" and "I am happy" welled up naturally. I think that it took three months to finally understand what the Dean said before my departure. To return to being a baby, to free myself from my earlier assumptions, to come out of my own shell. To be thankful for the people around me, for nature and for history. "There are only two ways to live your life. One is as though nothing is a miracle. The other is as though everything is a miracle." -Albert Einstein

The warmth of Philly. Philadelphia, an old American city on almost exactly the opposite side of the globe from Japan. The locals affectionately call their city "Philly." Finally, I will describe what I felt through my three months of life in Philly. I exchange greetings with the people of Philly. "Good morning," "You look well today, too." I talk with hospital staff and doctors. "Naomi, you've come from Japan, isn't it hard?" "I've been to Japan," "Japan is a wonderful place, isn't it." I talk with patients' families. "Welcome from so far away!" "Naomi, you came all the way from Japan to Philly, so enjoy yourself a lot," "A kind medical student like Naomi is more than welcome." These were all words said out of consideration for me. "Make yourself at home," I feel that they always took care so that I could spend my time comfortably. Some people, such as patients' families, must have had no room for such things. I felt the generosity of the people of Philly. For them this may simply be the natural way of treating others. But isn't this "basic" relationship between people something that is now being lost in Japan? Aren't there quite a few people who find dealing with others "annoying," "troublesome" or, in some cases, "frightening"? We show consideration for each other and treat each other with courtesy. From that, trust and gratitude also arise. I thought that we need to return once more to our roots and reexamine the bonds between people. The warmth I experienced in Philly. It was precisely because it was such a blessed, warm environment that I was able to come out of my shell and treat them with an honest heart. Truly, these three months were supported by many fortunate encounters.

Acknowledgments. I thank the faculty of Nagoya University who gave me this opportunity, Ms. 西尾 of the office who supported me, the seniors who built the path of study abroad, everyone at the University of Pennsylvania Global Health Programs, and Dr. Akira, our big brother in Philly, who was always looking out for us. To the doctors and hospital staff who looked after me during the clerkship, thank you so much for accepting me as a student. The children of CHOP, the babies of the ICN, I will never forget how hard you all tried. The strong and deep love of the families for their children opened my eyes. I am grateful. Finally, I thank my father, my mother and 拓也, who supported me at all times, whether I was happy or feeling weak. Thank you.
